newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb politicians assert control over army.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb politicians assert control over army.

text.p: Bosnian Serb political leaders, asserting control over an army in disarray, swore in new commanders on Sunday after sacking indicted war criminal Ratko Mladic and other top generals.
Obscure officers took an oath at a brief ceremony, officially sealing a decision announced over the weekend by Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic.
Blaming Western demands for Mladic's removal, Plavsic said she "regretted" the decision to replace the commander.

But analysts said international diplomacy helped encourage a split among Serb ranks that made Mladic's dismissal convenient for Bosnian Serb civilian leaders who were keen to settle a long-running dispute with the army.
"It was a perfect excuse," said on Serb political source, who asked not to be named.
A similar attempt to sack Mladic and his general staff failed last year, but diplomats and Serb political sources said it was likely civilian authorities would succeed this time.
More than 24 hours after the purge was announced, there was no sign the Bosnian Serb army was preparing to take action to block it, Serb military sources said.
Diplomats say Plavsic's order suits the Bosnian Serbs' powerful patron, Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
The Serbian president is anxious to show the West he is cooperating with the Bosnian peace process and no longer needs the army to counter the authority of the civilian leaders.
Milosevic, whose government steered and funded the Bosnian Serb army, once used the military to force obedience from Bosnian Serb political leaders who opposed concessions in peace negotiations.
But Milosevic has since signed a peace treaty which the Bosnian Serbs are obliged to accept and now keeps the Serb republic at arm's length as part of his post-war image as "peacemaker".
Western envoys have also made clear to Serb leaders that reconstruction aid will depend on adhering to the peace treaty, which bars Mladic and other war crimes suspects from holding public office.
The pugnacious Mladic, revered by ordinary Serbs as a war hero, has so far made no public response to Plavsic's order.
Military analysts say Mladic, though bitter about the outcome of the war, is unlikely to resist his forced retirement and has never shown interest in entering the political arena.
Despite public bluster, Mladic has tended to obey the wishes of his superiors in Belgrade, who transferred him to Croatia and later Bosnia during the four-year Yugoslav conflict.
He may continue to exert influence behind the scenes in the short term but the war is over and he has overseen the most important aspects of a post-war demilitarisation.
With the army facing serious financial difficulties, and with health problems of his own, a low-profile retirement may be an attractive escape for Mladic.
Preparing the ground for his departure, Belgrade media with ties to the government have cast doubt on his health and predicted his retirement for the past several weeks.
The dismissal illustrated a shift in the balance of power between the Serb army and civilian authorities since wartime leader Radovan Karadzic tried and failed to sack Mladic last year.
With the end of the Bosnian war a year ago, the Serb police -- under the command of civilian leaders -- has become the dominant force in Bosnia's Serb republic.
The army has been plagued by morale problems, desertion, and a lack of financial support since the tide of war turned in favour of their Moslem-Croat foes.
It was the second major change in Serb leadership since July, when Karadzic bowed to international pressure and stepped down as president.
Both Karadzic and Mladic have been charged by the U.N. tribunal with orchestrating the slaughter of Moslems from Srebrenica, sniping against Sarajevo civilians and the capture of U.N. peacekeepers.
